analysis.one_liner: Turns the naval oil reserves into a for-profit corporation to be sold to private investors.
analysis.headline: Introduced by a single senator with zero cosponsors, the bill died in the Senate Armed Services Committee without a hearing, vote, or floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would move the Naval Petroleum Reserves and Naval Oil Shale Reserves — federal oil properties held by the Defense Department — into a new for-profit government corporation run to maximize their value. Within five years the corporation would have to write a plan to sell the whole operation to private investors, with the sale proceeds going to the Treasury. Along the way, the corporation would be exempt from state taxes, federal procurement rules, and federal administrative procedure, and its workers would leave the civil service system. Congress would receive notice and an evaluation report before any sale, but would get no vote on it.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, private investors would gain the opportunity to buy a government-owned oil and oil-shale operation, and the Treasury would collect a one-time payment from the sale plus the corporation's annual revenues above its operating costs while it remained public. Private investors would acquire an asset that, while government-owned, was exempt from state and local taxation, federal acquisition rules, and administrative procedure requirements.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Private oil investors and the Treasury

how_it_helps.text: The reserves would be run by a corporation directed to explore, develop, and produce them so as to 'maximize the economic value of these properties to the Nation,' with prices set to maximize the financial return to the Government and all revenue beyond operating costs transferred annually to the Treasury.

Within five years the corporation would have to deliver a privatization plan — public stock offering, private placement, or merger — and could implement it only if it determined the sale would return at least the corporation's net present value, with a Comptroller General evaluation sent to Congress and proceeds deposited in the general fund of the Treasury.
Running the reserves would move out of the Department of Defense, though the corporation would still have to give priority to national security matters when the Secretary of Defense requested it.

analysis.who_pays: The public would permanently give up ownership of the naval petroleum and oil shale reserves — assets originally held for national security — trading an ongoing government revenue stream for a one-time sale payment whose adequacy the corporation itself would help judge. Federal employees running the reserves would be transferred out of the competitive civil service, with pay set by the corporation's CEO and jobs removable at will after a one-year protection. The corporation itself would operate free of federal procurement rules, administrative procedure, and state and local taxes.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, losing a publicly owned asset

drawbacks.text: The privatization sale would require only the President's approval and 60 days' notice to Congress; the Comptroller General's evaluation would be a report, not a binding check, so a valuable public asset could be sold without any congressional vote.
The corporation would decide, in consultation with other agencies, whether the sale returned at least its own net present value — meaning the seller largely judged whether the price was adequate.

Employees transferred from the Defense Department would leave the competitive civil service: the Chief Executive Officer could set pay outside the General Schedule and remove workers at will after a one-year protection, and the corporation would be exempt from federal administrative procedure and federal property and acquisition rules.

The bill would convert an ongoing public revenue stream (excess reserve revenues, up to $250 million a year retained for operations and the rest sent to the Treasury) into a one-time lump-sum payment, and permanently end public ownership of reserves held since early in the 20th century as insurance for naval fuel supply.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The corporatization model had a real logic: a commercially run entity maximizing the reserves' value could return more to the Treasury than a Pentagon bureaucracy did, and a well-priced sale would compensate taxpayers in present-value terms. But the safeguards were thin. The net-present-value floor depended on the seller's own determination, the President's approval was the only check, and Congress's role was limited to notice and a report. The costs fell on the public in the long run — loss of a strategic reserve and of future public revenue from a large oil position — and on transferred federal workers, who gave up civil-service pay and removal protections. Whether the one-time payment would truly make taxpayers whole is exactly the question the bill left to the corporation itself.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Armed Services Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Senator Dale Bumpers of Arkansas introduced the bill alone on January 26, 1996 and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Armed Services that same day; no cosponsors ever joined.
No further action of any kind is recorded — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — and the bill died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing happened, so nothing changed: the reserves stayed under the Department of Defense and no assets began moving toward private sale. If the bill's privatization endpoint is counted as a transfer of public oil assets to private investors, the public was better off with the bill dead; either way, the reserves were never debated or voted on.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public kept the reserves unchanged

for.name: Sen. Dale Bumpers
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill alone, delivered introductory remarks, and made no recorded follow-up push

against.name: Senate Armed Services Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction (chair: Sen. Strom Thurmond, R-SC)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral the day it was introduced and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; one Democrat introduced the bill, zero senators from either party signed on as cosponsors, and the Republican-led committee simply never acted.

industries.industry: Oil and gas investors and producers
industries.note: The bill's endpoint was the sale of the naval petroleum and oil shale reserves to private investors through a stock offering, private placement, or merger, transferring production and future profits from public to private hands. The required return of at least the corporation's net present value to the Treasury would partially offset the public's loss, but public ownership of a strategic reserve would end permanently.

Defense Department employees running the reserves would be transferred to the corporation outside the competitive civil service, with corporation-set pay and at-will removal after one year. That flexibility served the commercial model but stripped standard federal job and pay protections.

The corporation could condemn a nearby pipeline that refused to carry reserve petroleum without discrimination at reasonable rates, and could take pipeline rights-of-way by eminent domain. That use of government condemnation power would operate for the corporation's commercial benefit.
